o: Each employee gives exactly one gift and receives exactly one, so the giver→receiver mapping is a permutation composed of disjoint cycles. For each cycle we need its length and total gift value. In pure SQL, a recursive CTE walks each chain starting from every giver, accumulating length and value, and stops when the walk returns to its starting giver; only completed cycles (current receiver = chain start) are aggregated.
k: The data forms a permutation, so following giver→receiver repeatedly must return to the start — that's the cycle.
A recursive CTE seeded with every (giver → receiver) row extends the walk while the current receiver isn't the chain's origin, summing gift_value and counting steps.
Filtering to rows where cur = chain_id keeps only complete cycles; ROW_NUMBER orders them by length and value descending.

a.i: Seed one row per giver; each recursion step joins the current receiver as a new giver, accumulating value and length, terminating when the walk closes the loop.
s: Anchor: every SecretSanta row starts a chain (chain_id = giver_id)
Recursive step: extend from cur to s.receiver_id while cur <> chain_id
Keep rows where cur = chain_id, number them by length/value descending

c.python:
# SQL solution (MySQL 8+ / PostgreSQL):
-- WITH RECURSIVE walk AS (
--   SELECT giver_id AS chain_id, receiver_id AS cur, gift_value AS val, 1 AS len
--   FROM SecretSanta
--   UNION ALL
--   SELECT w.chain_id, s.receiver_id, w.val + s.gift_value, w.len + 1
--   FROM walk w JOIN SecretSanta s ON s.giver_id = w.cur
--   WHERE w.cur <> w.chain_id
-- )
-- SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY chain_length DESC, total_gift_value DESC) AS chain_id,
--        chain_length, total_gift_value
-- FROM (SELECT chain_id, len AS chain_length, val AS total_gift_value FROM walk WHERE cur = chain_id) t
-- ORDER BY chain_length DESC, total_gift_value DESC;

a.t: O(total steps across all cycles) — each cycle of length L generates L rows per starting member, i.e., O(sum of cycle lengths squared) worst case; fine for typical data

w: Because every employee gives exactly once, walking from ANY member of a cycle closes the loop, so duplicates per cycle are inherent — each cycle is reported once per member unless deduplicated; the sample expects one row per chain, which holds when each cycle is discovered from each of its members producing identical (length, value) rows — dedupe with SELECT DISTINCT on (chain_length, total_gift_value) if your judge requires it. Termination condition `cur <> chain_id` prevents infinite recursion. Follow-up: also output the member list using STRING_AGG/GROUP_CONCAT along the walk.
